newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australian dlr resolute despite rate dilemma.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australian dlr resolute despite rate dilemma.

text.p: The Australian dollar drifted up to a steady, if anti-climactic, close Wednesday as long-feared inflation figures failed to settle the market's rate dilemma.

The widely held judgement was the data left the door open for an easing, but were not compelling enough on their own to push the Reserve Bank through. But it may yet take the step if Q3 wages data on Thursday were subdued enough to soothe the bank's concerns on private sector pay growth, traders said.
"Today's data would not stand on the way of a rate cut, but it doesn't make one inevitable either," summed up Bruce Freeland, chief economist at Commonwealth Bank.
By 5.00 pm (0700 GMT) the local dollar was resting at US$0.7951/56 after inching up from an early US$0.7939/44, to stand little changed from Tuesday's late US$0.7955/60.
Support proved solid at US$0.7940, and more was expected at US$0.7910, while resistance lined up at US$0.7990 and US$0.8020.
It also bounced on the yen to 89.60/70 from an opening 89.07/17, leaving it a shade higher on Tuesday's late 89.50/60.

The rally was partly attributed to direct Japanese demand linked to samurai issues and partly to a smart recovery by the U.S. dollar which took it to 112.70/75 yen from 112.10/15. In trade weighted terms it ended at 58.8 from a previous 58.9.
The currency's early softness reflected speculation the September quarter inflation figures would be so weak the RBA would be hard pressed to justify not easing policy.
In the event the inflation slowdown was much in line with market forecasts and probably close to what the RBA had expected when it last cut official rates to 7.0 percent on July 31.

Underlying inflation rose a modest 0.5 percent in the September quarter while the annual rate receded to 2.4 percent from 3.1 percent in Q2. That was the lowest reading since March 1995 and back within the RBA's 2-3 percent target range only a couple of quarters after peaking at 3.3 percent.
The headline consumer price index rose by 0.3 percent on the quarter, exactly as expected, while the annual rate plunged to a two-year low of 2.1 percent from 3.1 percent in Q2.
Falls in mortgage interest charges, petrol prices, motor vehicles and furniture contributed most to the subdued result.
For all that, analysts felt it was not low enough on its own to trigger an immediate cut in domestic interest rates given the RBA's recently voiced concerns about future wages growth.
"Despite the confirmation of low inflation, the outlook for monetary policy is dependant upon the wages data released tomorrow," said Bankers Trust senior economist Peter Munckton.
Third quarter average weekly ordinary time earnings (AWOTE), out Thursday, should rise 1.0 percent but that would still see annual growth slow to 3.7 percent from 3.9 percent in Q2.
This would be well below the RBA's danger level of 4.5 percent and confirm the slowing trend in overall wage claims.
"A good wages number, combined with the low inflation and subdued activity data we have seen in recent times, would set the platform for another cut in rates," said Munckton.
The 90-day bank bill future reflected an element of doubt by falling four basis points to 93.38, but that still implied a rate of 6.62 percent by year end from 7.00 percent at present.
Some dealers even entertained the heretical thought that one more rate cut might not actually matter much for the dollar.
"The one certainty in all this is that if a cut comes, it will be the definite, absolute, unarguable end of the easing cycle here," said one.
The dollar would still be offering a healthy yield premium to Japanese and other offshore investors and it looked likely Japanese and U.S. rates were on hold until 1997, he said.
"It might not agree with the textbooks, but I wouldn't be surprised if the Aussie actually rallied once a cut was out the way." -- Wayne Cole 61-2 9373 1800
